author: Isaac Gantwerk Mayer (transcription & naqdanut)

coauthors.name: Isaac Gantwerk Mayer (transcription & naqdanut)
coauthors.bio: From a family of musicians, Isaac Gantwerk Mayer believes that creative art is one of the most powerful ways to get in touch with the divine. He composes music and poetry in Hebrew and English. (He also translates and authors his own original works.) Isaac runs a Jewish music transcription service, which will transcribe and set any Jewish music in any language, recorded or written. Contact his service on Facebook or via his music blog.

coauthors.name: Reuven Eliyahu Yisrael (translation)
coauthors.bio: Reuven Eliyahu Yisrael (1856-1932) of Craiova from a long line of rabbinic leaders in Rhodes, was the last chief rabbi of the island. Rabbi Israel devoted a great part of his life to the translation in Ladino (Judeo-Spanish) of psalms, proverbs, poems and religious works, such as the “Kryiat de Izhak” (The Sacrifice of Isaac) and the Pirqei Avot. He served as Shaliah Tsibbur and ritual slaughterer in Rhodes for 18 years; traveled to Shuman, Bulgaria and from there to Craiova, Romania where he served as cantor and rabbi for 24 ½ years; spent the last 10 years of his life as Rabbi in Rhodes. On his last vist to Rhodes in the 1920's King Vittorio Emanuele of Italy bestowed on him the title of Knight of the Crown of Italy.

coauthors.name: Ephraim bar Isaac of Regensburg
coauthors.bio: Ephraim ben Isaac ben Abraham of Regensburg (אפרים בן יצחק מרגנסבורג, a/k/a Ben Yakir; ca. 1110–1175), born in Regensburg, Germany was a German tosafist and liturgical poet known for his keen intellect, numerous piyyutim, and for controversy refusing to recognize any post-Talmudic authority. In his early years, he studied under Isaac ben Mordecai and Isaac ben Asher ha-Levi, later moving to France to study under Rabbeinu Tam of whom he was an early student. On his return from France he settled in his birth-town of Regensburg, where, along with Isaac ben Mordecai and Moses ben Abraham, he established a rabbinical collegium. It was also during this time that he served as a respected member of the Regensburg bet din. Ephraim wrote tosafot to various Talmudic treatises, some portions of which may be found in the printed tosafot as well as in other works. He wrote a commentary on Pirkei Avot and halakhic decisioning. He also apparently wrote "Arba Panim" a commentary on Seder Nezikin. Ephraim also employed the metric forms of Sephardi poetry and one of his seliḥot is in the Sephardi festival liturgy. Of apparent remarkable keenness of perception, he refused to recognize, either in the theoretical or in the practical field, any post-Talmudic authority, and often, therefore, came into conflict with his teachers and colleagues. Once, after a particularly heated dispute with the rabbis of Speyer, Rabbenu Tam answered Rabbi Ephraim sharply stating: "From the day I have known you, I have never heard you concede a point." Rabbenu Tam, however, appreciating Ephraim's selfless motives, bore him no ill will, even referring to him affectionately as "my brother Rabbi Ephraim." Another time, Rabbi Ephraim tried to introduce extensive modifications to the strict Passover regulations, in spite of the protest of Rabbi Ephraim ben Joseph, whose authority he refused to recognize. However Rabbi Ephraim is probably best known for abrogating established customs and religious regulations which had been long regarded as inviolable, because he saw no reason for their existence to be found in the Talmud. Despite his controversial nature, his halakic literature was still greatly respected and still achieved great success. He is considered by some as the greatest writer of piyyutim of his time. Over thirty two of his piyyutim are extant, many of which reflect the hardships suffered by the Jews of Germany in the Regensburg massacre of 1137 and during the Second Crusade. He later moved on to Worms, and then back to Regensburg, where he died.

excerpt: Im Afes Rova' ha-Qen, an Aqedah (poetic retelling of the binding of Isaac) written by the 12th-century scholar R. Ephraim ben Isaac of Regensburg, is one of the few piyyuṭim of Ashkenazi origin to have a beloved place in the Sephardic liturgy. (Much more commonly things go the other way.) In current Sephardic practice it is recited every single weeknight in the month of Elul, as part of the seliḥot liturgy — as well as on the second day of Rosh haShanah. It is also recited in most Ashkenazi Seliḥot liturgies — in the Bohemian and Lithuanian customs on the fast of Gedaliah, and in the Polish custom on the fourth day of the ten days. Which means that not only is this Ashkenazi piyyuṭ beloved by Sephardim, it is substantially *more* beloved by Sephardim than it is by Ashkenazim! And as with any beloved piyyuṭ, it has been translated into the colloquial for all the people to appreciate its language. The following is not only the complete Hebrew text of Im Afes along with a new English translation, but also a rhyming Ladino translation composed by R. Reuven Eliyahu Yisrael, the spiritual leader of the Sephardic community of Craiova, Romania, and published in the aforementioned town in the year 1910 (in טראדוקסייון ליברי די לאס פואיזיאס איבראיקאאס). To demonstrate the techniques used by R. Yisrael in his translation, a literal translation of the Ladino, as well as a transcription into the Latin-script Aki Yerushalaim orthography, is also provided.
content:
Im Afes Rova’ ha-Qen, an Aqedah (poetic retelling of the binding of Isaac) written by the 12th-century scholar R. Ephraim ben Isaac of Regensburg, is one of the few piyyuṭim of Ashkenazi origin to have a beloved place in the Sephardic liturgy. (Much more commonly things go the other way.) In current Sephardic practice it is recited every single weeknight in the month of Elul, as part of the seliḥot liturgy — as well as on the second day of Rosh haShanah. It is also recited in most Ashkenazi Seliḥot liturgies — in the Bohemian and Lithuanian customs on the fast of Gedaliah, and in the Polish custom on the fourth day of the ten days. Which means that not only is this Ashkenazi piyyuṭ beloved by Sephardim, it is substantially *more* beloved by Sephardim than it is by Ashkenazim! And as with any beloved piyyuṭ, it has been translated into the colloquial for all the people to appreciate its language.

The following is not only the complete Hebrew text of Im Afes along with a new English translation, but also a rhyming Ladino translation composed by R. Reuven Eliyahu Yisrael, the spiritual leader of the Sephardic community of Craiova, Romania, and published in the aforementioned town in the year 1910 (in טראדוקסייון ליברי די לאס פואיזיאס איבראיקאאס). To demonstrate the techniques used by R. Yisrael in his translation, a literal translation of the Ladino, as well as a transcription into the Latin-script Aki Yerushalaim orthography, is also provided.

and God saw all that he did.[13] Genesis 1:31 
לו קי איזו איסטי פאדרי אזי אינקאנטאר,
סין נינגונה פיאדאד אה סו איזﬞו איבﬞה קורטאר,
פארה אלייגארלו סאקריפﬞיסייו סובﬞרי איל אלטאר,
פור איגזיקוטיר איל אורדין די סו דייו אי ריספיקטאר.
Lo ke izo este padre aze enkantar
sin ninguna peadad, a su ijo iva kortar,
para ayegarlo sakrifisio sovre el altar,
por egzekutir el orden de su Dio i respektar.
What this father did was shocking:
without any mercy, he was going to cut down his son,
to offer him as a sacrifice on the altar,
to carry out the order of his God and to respect it.
קָרָא מֵרֶ֣חֶם מִשְׁחָ֑ר
תְּמוּר בִּנְךָ הַנִּבְחָר
וְהִנֵּה אַֽיִל אַחַר
וַעֲשֵׂ֖ה אַל־תְּאַחַ֑ר׃
They called, “Dawn’s wombed![14] An expression from Psalms 110:3, which, according to Bereshit Rabbah 39:8, refers to Abraham. 
There is a substitute for your chosen son.
And here is a ram back there!
And do so, do not delay!”[15] Daniel 9:19 
קואנדו אברהם מיטיאה איל קוגﬞיאו אין לה גארגאנטה,
אונה בוז דיל סיילו לייאמאבﬞה אה בוז אלטה:
אברהם! אברהם! נו טוקיס אל משנסיבﬞו, באסטה!
דיגוייה איסטי בארבﬞיז אי אה יצחק דיזאטה.
Kuando Avraam metia el cochio en la garganta,
una boz del sielo yamava a boz alta:
Avraam, Avraam! no tokes al mansebo, basta!
degoya a ese barvez y a Yishak dezata.
As Abraham put the knife to his throat,
a voice from heaven called out aloud:
“Abraham, Abraham! Do not touch the young man, stop,
Slit the throat of that ram and untie Isaac.
חֲלִיפֵי אַזְכָּרָתוֹ
תִּכּוֹן כְּהַקְטָרָתוֹ
וְתַעֲלֶה לְךָ תִּמְרָתוֹ
וְהָֽיָה־ה֥וּא וּתְמוּרָת֖וֹ׃
Establish replacements for his memorial
as if it were him who was smoking.
And let its fumes raise to You
to be him and his substitution.[16] Leviticus 27:10 
איסטי אנימאל סיאה סו רימפלאסאמיינטו,
דיסטינאדו פארה איסטו דיזדי סו נאסימיינטו,
לייה קונוסי לה פוריזה די טו סינטימיינטו,
טו פﬞידילידאד אי טו דיבﬞואמיינטו.
Este animal seya su remplasamyento,
destinado para esto dezde su nasimyento,
ya konosi la pureza de tu sentimyento,
tu fedelidad i tu devuamyento.
This animal is to be his replacement,
destined for this since birth.
Already I knew the purity of your feeling,
your loyalty and your devotion.”
זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנֶֽיךָ בַּשַּֽׁחַק
לָעַד בַּסֵּֽפֶר יוּחַק
בְּרִית עוֹלָם בַּל־יֻמְחַק
אֶת־אַבְרָהָם וְאֶת־יִצְחָק׃
Remembrance before You in the welkin,
forever inscribed in the Book,
an eternal covenant never erased,
with Abraham and with Isaac[17] Exodus 2:24, with additional “and” 
לה מימורייה די איסטי אקסו, סיאה, או דייו, דילאנטרי די טו סיאה!
פאדרי אי איזﬞו טו אובﬞידיסיירון קון גראנדי אינירזﬞיאה,
נו אולבﬞידיס טו אליאנסה קון לה נאסייון זﬞודיאה,
אוליי נואיסטראס אוראסייוניס אין איסטי דיאה.
La memoria de este akto, seya, o Dio, delantre de tu sia!
Padre i ijo te ovedisyeron kon grande enerjia,
no olvides tu aliansa kon la nasyon judia,
oyi nuestras orasyones en este dia.
May the memory of this act, o God, be before Your throne!
Father and son obeyed You with great energy.
Do not forget Your covenant with the Jewish nation;
hear our prayers on this day!
קֹרְאֶֽיךָ בָּאִים לָקֹד
בְּצָרָה עֲקֵדָה תִּשְׁקֹד
וְצֹאנְךָ בְּרַחֲמִים תִּפְקֹד
פְּנֵ֨י הַצֹּ֧אן אֶל־עָקֹ֛ד׃
Those calling to You come to bow,
in stress. Care for the binding,
and consider Your flock in compassion,
the flock facing to the binding.[18] Genesis 30:40 
טוס איזﬞוס פﬞידיליס טו יאמאן קון אבאטיסייון,
איסטי אקטו אימפורטאנטי סיאה סוס מאמפאראסייון,
ריזגאטה קון טוס פיאדאדיס אה טו נאסייון,
קי איספירה סיימפרי טו סאלבﬞאסייון.
Tus ijos fedeles te yaman kon abatisyon,
este akto emportante sea sus mamparasyon,
rezgata kon tus piadades a tu nasyon,
ke espera siempre tu salvasyon.
Your faithful children call to you in desperation.
May this important act be their protection;
rescue with Your mercy Your nation
that always awaits your salvation.
עוֹרְרָה גְבוּרָתְךָ לְהָקִיץ נִרְדָּמִים
לְמַעַנְךָ תִּפְדֶּה חֲרֵדִים נִדְהָמִים
לְהַמְשִׁיךְ רַחֲמֶֽיךָ וַחֲסָדֶֽיךָ מִשְּׁמֵי מְרוֹמִים
אֵל מֶֽלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב עַל־כִּסֵּא רַחֲמִים׃
Rouse Your might to awaken the sleepers,
for Your sake redeem the quaking astonished ones,
to extend Your compassion and grace from the highest heavens:
Sovereign Deity, seated on a throne of compassion![19] This final verse, which introduces the recitation of the thirteen attributes in the context of Sephardic seliḥot, does not have a parallel in the translation.
